Hi, I'm Joel Fernandes at Moss & Finch (joel@mossfinch.example). We started with three people, then hired two coordinators, and now client documents arrive in several inboxes. We tried folders, labels, and a spreadsheet, but the sheet gets out of date whenever someone replaces a file. We are planning our next busy season and I have been asked to compare tools before the team adds more clients. I have talked with finance about a first-year limit of ₹75,000, although setup charges may need separate approval. I am probably giving too much context, but the main question is simple: what is the annual price for a 10-user plan, including setup? We hope to select a tool next month, so a written estimate would help.

Hello Northstar Docs team,

My name is Meera Kapoor and I run operations at Cedar & Finch, a small compliance consultancy that has grown faster than we expected over the last two years. I am writing from my personal inbox because our shared mailbox is being reorganized, and I hope that is all right. You can reach me at meera.kapoor@cedarfinch.example. I am trying to understand whether your document intake product could fit our next phase, and I will probably give more background than you need because I am putting my thoughts in one place before I speak with our partners.

When we started, there were only four of us and every client sent files to one person. We could keep a paper checklist beside the printer and remember which document belonged to which engagement. Today there are twenty three people, several contractors, and a rotating group of reviewers. Some of our clients send a few documents every month, while others send a large packet at the beginning of an audit. The process that was fine for a tiny team has become fragile, even though nobody has had time to step back and redesign it.

Our current process is a mixture of email, folders, and spreadsheets. A client sends a message to an account manager, the account manager saves the attachments, and then somebody adds a row to a tracker. The reviewer downloads a copy, adds comments, and sends it back. If the client replaces one page, we sometimes end up with two files that have almost the same name. That is not a dramatic crisis, but it creates a steady stream of small questions that interrupt more important work. I am collecting those examples so that we can explain the change to the team.

We do not need a large enterprise platform with dozens of modules. We need a reliable place for incoming documents, a way to see what is missing, and a record of who reviewed each item. A few people have asked whether we should build a custom workflow in our own tools. I am cautious about that because we already maintain several internal spreadsheets, and those sheets depend on one or two people remembering how they work. My preference is to buy a focused service if the price is sensible and the service does not create another fragile process.

The work is seasonal. At the busiest time, two or three client projects begin in the same week, and then we receive a concentrated set of forms and statements. In a quiet month, the volume is much lower. I do not have a clean count because our current tracker is not consistent, but a normal client might send between twenty and sixty files during an engagement. We could make a rough estimate from last year's folders, although I would want someone to check it before we use it for a final quote.

We have different kinds of documents, but they are mostly ordinary office files: PDFs, spreadsheets, and photographs of signed pages. Some clients still scan documents in a way that makes the text hard to search. We do not want the service to make business decisions for us. A reviewer must still confirm that a document is present and that the information appears complete. The software should reduce the chasing and sorting, while leaving the judgment with our staff.

We also have a few access questions. A project lead should be able to invite a client contact to upload files for one engagement, while a reviewer should see only the work assigned to that reviewer. Our partners need a high level view of active projects. We have not agreed on every detail, so I am not asking for a design proposal in this first email. I mention it because our team is likely to ask about access as soon as we talk about changing the process.

The people who would use a new service are not all technical. Some are comfortable with new software and some prefer a short checklist with clear labels. We would need a simple first week, perhaps a small pilot with two clients and a handful of internal reviewers. If the pilot is confusing, people will go back to email and the old tracker. That is why ease of adoption matters at least as much as a long feature list.

I have talked with two operations managers at other firms. One said that her team spent a lot of time checking whether clients had sent the latest version. Another said they had solved that with a shared folder, but she could not tell me how they handled access when a contractor left. Those conversations were useful but not conclusive. We serve different client types, and what works for a larger firm may be too complicated for us.

Our partners will ask about cost in a practical way. They are not expecting a bargain product to solve every process problem, but they will want to know what the first year costs and what happens if volume grows. If there is a setup fee, I would like to see it separated from the recurring price. If seats, storage, or processed files affect the total, please show the assumptions so that we can compare them with our current time spent on administration.

I have a preliminary budget of about ₹50,000 for the first year of a small pilot and initial rollout. That number is not a procurement approval and may change when we review it with finance. We could probably request more if the product saves meaningful staff time, but I do not want to imply that the amount is unlimited. If your normal package is far above that, it would still help to know the approximate range so we can make a sensible decision rather than spend several weeks on calls.

There are a few dates in the background. We renew two client agreements in about three weeks, and our partners would like to decide whether to change the intake process before that work starts. The decision is not an emergency today. I would rather get a clear picture than rush into a tool, but it would be useful to understand the available plans soon enough to include the cost in our next planning meeting.

I have not yet prepared a formal requirements document. I have a collection of notes from staff meetings, a spreadsheet of recurring issues, and a list of questions from the partners. Some of those notes overlap, and a few are probably solutions disguised as requirements. For example, one colleague wants an automatic reminder every morning, while another prefers a weekly summary. We should sort out the actual problem before deciding which notification pattern is best.

Our current spreadsheet has columns for client, engagement, document type, requested date, received date, reviewer, and status. It has no consistent way to link a replacement file to the version it replaced. We have tried color coding, but color means different things to different people and the sheet is difficult to read when printed. A centralized status view might help, though we would still need to train people to update it when something changes.

We are also careful about client confidentiality. Some projects include financial records and identity documents, so we need to understand how data is stored and who can access it. I am not asking you to answer every security question in a pricing reply. A clear description of the standard plan and a link to the normal security information would be enough for an initial discussion. We would bring our compliance lead into a later review if the commercial fit looks reasonable.

I sometimes get ahead of myself when I write these messages. The short version is that our team has outgrown a shared inbox and a spreadsheet, but we do not yet know whether a dedicated document intake service will be more efficient. I have included several side topics because they are the questions people raise in meetings, not because every one must be solved before we can compare plans. The first useful step is probably to learn the price range and the limits of the standard package.

We have considered hiring a temporary coordinator for the busy season. That could help with downloading and renaming files, but it would not fix the question of which version is current. We have also discussed asking clients to use a single upload link. That may reduce email attachments, but without a clear view of what is still missing we would continue to maintain the spreadsheet. I am not trying to dismiss either option; I just want to compare the total effort over a full year.

Our expected growth is modest. We may add a few staff members next quarter, and there is a chance that one existing client will expand its work with us. We are not expecting hundreds of users or millions of documents. A plan aimed at a very large organization would probably be excessive. On the other hand, we do not want to select a package that becomes unsuitable after a small increase in volume, so any limits on seats or monthly files would be useful to know.

The partners have different preferences. One wants a short demonstration before looking at numbers, another wants a written estimate first, and a third is mostly concerned about whether clients can use the workflow without training. I am coordinating their questions, but I cannot promise that we will move forward until they have reviewed the options. A clear pricing page or a concise quote with the important assumptions would let me bring the conversation to them without misrepresenting what is included.

I am sending this during a week with several deadlines, so I may not reply immediately if you ask for a long questionnaire. Email is the easiest way to reach me. A short response with the relevant package, indicative annual cost, and any volume assumptions would be helpful. If pricing depends on details that I have not provided, please tell me the two or three facts that would change the estimate most, and I can check them with our operations coordinator.

One last detail: the ₹50,000 figure is the approximate first year amount we can currently set aside for a small pilot and rollout, not a promise that the product should be priced exactly at that amount. We would need to compare the total with staff time and the risk of continuing with the current process. I realize I have circled back to cost more than once; that is because it is the first question the partners asked me to answer.

Another thing I have learned from trying to organize this is that our internal vocabulary is inconsistent. One person calls a signed statement a form, another calls it a declaration, and a client may use the name of the department that requested it. This sounds like a small issue, but it makes the tracker less useful when somebody is covering for a colleague. We would want to begin with a plain set of document types and let people ask for an exception when a client uses something unusual. I do not expect the software to guess every synonym correctly, and I would rather have a clear manual step than an impressive demo that hides mistakes. We have not measured this carefully, so the estimate of time saved is still a hypothesis. If the pricing is within reach, we could run a short pilot and record how often staff need to correct a status or chase a missing item. That would give us a practical basis for expanding the rollout.

Could you share the pricing for the smallest plan that would suit a team of about twenty three people, including any setup fee and the main file or seat limits? If that plan is above our preliminary ₹50,000 first year pilot budget, an approximate range for the next suitable option would still help us decide whether to schedule a discussion. We are hoping to choose a direction before the client work begins in about three weeks.

Thanks,
Meera Kapoor
